newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: SOCCER - HOSTS UAE FACE TOUGH ASIAN CUP OPENER.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER - HOSTS UAE FACE TOUGH ASIAN CUP OPENER.

text.p: Hosts the United Arab Emirates take on South Korea in the opening game of the 11th Asian Cup on Wednesday hoping that history and home advantage will give them the edge over one of the favourites.
In six of the past 10 championships the host nation has won the Asian title.

But the UAE face a well organised and experienced South Korean team who have won the title twice, and lost in three other finals, in the competition's 40-year history. The South Koreans also performed strongly at the 1994 World Cup, drawing against Spain 2-2 and narrowly losing 2-3 to then-champions Germany.

South Korea won all their qualifying matches, scoring 17 times without reply. They hope top striker Ko Jeong Woon, who is moving to Japan's J-league next season, will remain fit throughout the competition after a recent run of injuries.
The UAE are coached by experienced Croat Tomoslav Ivic who took Portugal's Porto to victory in the world club championship in 1987. He has also coached top European clubs Ajax and Marseille.
The opening Group A clash in Abu Dhabi will be followed by a meeting between the group's two other teams, Kuwait and Indonesia.

Kuwait, title winners in 1980, enter the competition on a high after their surprise victory in a Gulf Arab tournament in October where they outshone the UAE and Saudi Arabia, one of the front runners for the Asian Cup.
Indonesia are one of two newcomers to the finals and their chances of making an impact look slim.

The 12 finalists, the largest number in the history of the competition, are divided into three groups with the winners and runners-up of each group plus the best two teams in third place qualifying for the quarter-finals.

Group B promises to provide the most intriguing matches, with the shadow of politics weighing heavily over many of the games. It groups former battlefield foes Saudi Arabia, Iraq and Iran with Thailand.
Holders Japan, China, Syria and newcomers Uzbekistan make up Group C where the Japanese and China are expected to dominate.
Japan, ranked 20th in the world, are Asia's top team and the favourites for the title.

The Asian Football Confederation, which has steered the tournament away from many political minefields in the past four decades, is hoping Kuwait and Iraq will not be drawn against each other after the first stage.
Kuwait have indicated that they will pull out of the competition rather than play against former occupiers Iraq.
